citations.quote: A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

derivations.claim: By [F2], both finite path spaces carry their stated product sigma-algebras and the target path space is standard Borel. Fix a prefix $z_{0:t-1}$. The append map $j_{z_{0:t-1}}(z_t)=(z_{0:t-1},z_t)$ is measurable: the inverse image of a generating rectangle is either empty or the final-coordinate measurable set, and [F3] generates the target sigma-algebra from these rectangles. Thus $A\mapsto M_t(z_{t-1},j_{z_{0:t-1}}^{-1}(A))$ is the pushforward of the probability measure $M_t(z_{t-1},\cdot)$ and is a probability measure.

The projection $z_{0:t-1}\mapsto z_{t-1}$ is measurable, so composing each set-evaluation map $z_{t-1}\mapsto M_t(z_{t-1},B)$ with this projection gives a probability kernel from the prefix space to $\mathsf Z_t$. The function $(z_{0:t-1},z_t)\mapsto\mathbf1_A(z_{0:t-1},z_t)$ is product-measurable. By [F5], its integral against this composed kernel is measurable in the prefix. Together with step 1.1, this proves that $\overline M_t$ has probability-measure sections and measurable set evaluations, hence is a probability kernel. Iterating the definition appends each state using exactly $M_t$ because at each step the indicator is evaluated on the already fixed prefix and the new coordinate.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $Z_t$ take values in a standard-Borel space
$(\mathsf Z_t,\mathcal Z_t)$ and let $U_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t}$ for a finite
horizon $0\le t\le T$. For $1\le t\le T$, let
$Y_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t}$; observations begin at time $1$. The nonlinear
component has initial probability $\mu_0$ and transition probability kernels
$M_t(z_{t-1},dz_t)$; its transition does not depend on $U_{t-1}$. Given the
entire nonlinear path $z_{0:T}$, write $\mathsf Z_{0:t}=\prod_{s=0}^t\mathsf Z_s$
with its finite-product sigma-algebra and specify Borel maps
$$m_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0},\qquad P_0:\mathsf Z_0\to\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0},$$
and, for $1\le t\le T$,
$$A_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}},\quad Q_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t},\quad C_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t},\quad R_t:\mathsf Z_{0:t}\to\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}.$$
Require $P_0(z_0)$ and
$Q_t(z_{0:t})$ to be symmetric positive semidefinite, meaning
$v^TPv\ge0$ for every matching vector $v$, and $R_t(z_{0:t})$ to be
positive definite, meaning $v^TR_tv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Conditional
on $Z_{0:T}=z_{0:T}$, the linear component and observations have the finite
linear-Gaussian model, with the transition and observation equations for
$1\le t\le T$:
$$U_0\sim N(m_0(z_0),P_0(z_0)),\qquad U_t=A_t(z_{0:t})U_{t-1}+\xi_t,\qquad Y_t=C_t(z_{0:t})U_t+\varepsilon_t,$$
where the centered Gaussian noises $\xi_t\sim N(0,Q_t(z_{0:t}))$ and
$\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,R_t(z_{0:t}))$ are mutually independent over time
and independent of $U_0$, under that conditional law. For every fixed path
$z_{0:T}$ these are exactly the hypotheses of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
deterministic matrices.

This hierarchical conditionally linear-Gaussian model is the input class for
the Rao–Blackwellized filter below: it samples the nonlinear path and keeps
the conditional Gaussian law of $U_t$ analytically. It does not include a
nonlinear transition whose law depends on $U_{t-1}$, nor does it assert that
the marginal nonlinear process remains Markov after conditioning on all
observations. Such models need their own marginal transition and backward
kernels. A state-space filtering or smoothing law is a data-indexed regular
conditional-distribution version as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]; no pointwise uniqueness on null data
histories is imposed.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Assume AC. Let $U\in\mathbb R^d$, $q\in\mathbb R^n$, and
$r\in\mathbb R^p$ be mutually independent Gaussian vectors with
$$U\sim N_d(m,P),\qquad q\sim N_n(0,Q),\qquad r\sim N_p(0,R),$$
where $P,Q,R$ are symmetric positive semidefinite. Let
$F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$, and set
$$X=FU+q,\qquad Y=HX+r,\qquad P^-:=FPF^T+Q,\qquad S:=HP^-H^T+R.$$
If $S$ is positive definite, put $K:=P^-H^TS^{-1}$. Then $(X,Y)$ is jointly
Gaussian with mean $(Fm,HFm)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}P^-&P^-H^T\\HP^-&S\end{pmatrix},$$
and for every $y\in\mathbb R^p$ an everywhere-defined conditional law is
$$\mathcal L(X\mid Y=y)=N_n\!\left(Fm+K(y-HFm),\,P^--KSK^T\right).$$
The conditional covariance is positive semidefinite even if $P$, $Q$, or
$R$ is singular. It also equals the Joseph expression
$$ (I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^T+KRK^T.$$
No inverse of a state, process-noise, or measurement-noise covariance is
used.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Let $T\ge0$ be finite, let $(\mathsf Z_t,\mathcal Z_t)$ be standard-Borel
spaces for $0\le t\le T$, and for $1\le t\le T$ let
$M_t:\mathsf Z_{t-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf Z_t$ be probability kernels,
with the kernel convention of
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. For $1\le t\le T$, define the path-extension kernel
from $\mathsf Z_{0:t-1}$ to $\mathsf Z_{0:t}$ by
$$\overline M_t(z_{0:t-1},A)=\int_{\mathsf Z_t}\mathbf1_A(z_{0:t-1},z_t)M_t(z_{t-1},dz_t).$$
Then $\overline M_t$ is a probability kernel and $\mathsf Z_{0:t}$ is
standard Borel. Its ordered iterates append the nonlinear states with the
original transition law.

derivations.claim: Initially $P_{0|0}=P_0(z_0)$ is positive semidefinite. If $P_{t-1|t-1}$ is positive semidefinite, then $P_{t|t-1}=A_tP_{t-1|t-1}A_t^T+Q_t$ is positive semidefinite because $u^TP_{t|t-1}u=(A_t^Tu)^TP_{t-1|t-1}(A_t^Tu)+u^TQ_tu\ge0$. For every nonzero observation vector $a$, $a^TS_ta=(C_t^Ta)^TP_{t|t-1}(C_t^Ta)+a^TR_ta>0$, since the first term is nonnegative and $R_t$ is positive definite. Induction proves all innovation matrices meet the Kalman algorithm's domain.

By [F1], for this fixed path the conditional model is the deterministic finite-horizon model of [F2]. Step 1.1 verifies its positive-innovation hypothesis, so [F2] gives the exact conditional Gaussian filter at every observation history, including singular state covariances. At each time, [F3] gives the marginal observation law $N(C_tm_{t|t-1},S_t)$; applying [F4] yields the displayed density.

The coefficient functions are Borel by [F1]. Finite sums and products preserve Borel measurability, and matrix inversion and determinant are continuous on the positive-definite matrices established in step 1.1. The Kalman moment recursion and the displayed density are therefore Borel functions of the path. The covariance determinant is finite and positive and the exponential is finite and strictly positive, so $\ell_t$ has the claimed range.

For a fixed nonlinear path, step 2.1 gives the one-step conditional density $\ell_s$ of $Y_s$ given $Y_{1:s-1}$. By the defining event-integral identity for conditional densities, $p(y_{1:s}\mid z)=p(y_{1:s-1}\mid z)\ell_s(z_{0:s};y_{1:s})$ on finite-positive fibers; induction from the empty history, whose density is one, gives the product $\prod_{s=1}^t\ell_s$. By [F7], the ordered path-extension kernels are probability kernels on the standard-Borel path spaces and give the nonlinear path law. The joint law of $Z_{0:t}$ and $Y_{1:t}$ therefore has this product as its observation-density factor relative to that path law and Lebesgue observation measure. By [F5], conditioning on a history with finite positive evidence weights the nonlinear path law by this product and divides by its integral. Comparing with [F6] gives exactly the stated normalized Feynman–Kac path measure. This assertion is restricted to those finite-positive evidence fibers; null and infinite fibers are not normalized.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Assume AC and a finite-horizon model as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. For each $1\le t\le T$, let
$\nu_t$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ and suppose the
observation kernel has a specified product-measurable density
$g_t:E_t\times F_t\to[0,\infty]$ with respect to $\mathcal E_t\otimes\mathcal F_t$:
$$G_t(x,B)=\int_B g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy),\qquad\int_{F_t}g_t(x,y)\,\nu_t(dy)=1$$
for every state $x\in E_t$ and measurable $B\subseteq F_t$. For
$h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, let $\pi_{t-1}$ be the filtering kernel at time
$t-1$ from
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] when $t>1$, and for $t=1$ let $\pi_0$ be
the initial kernel $\mu_0$ on the singleton empty-history space. For
$A\in\mathcal E_t$, define the predictive kernel
$$\widehat\pi_t(h,A):=\int_{E_{t-1}}K_t(x,A)\,\pi_{t-1}(h,dx),$$
the evidence density
$$z_t(h,y):=\int_{E_t}g_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx),$$
and for $h\in\mathsf F_{1:t-1}$, $y\in F_t$, and $A\in\mathcal E_t$ define
the update
$$\pi_t(h,y,A):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ag_t(x,y)\,\widehat\pi_t(h,dx)}{z_t(h,y)},&0<z_t(h,y)<\infty,\\[6pt]\widehat\pi_t(h,A),&z_t(h,y)=0\text{ or }z_t(h,y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\pi_t$ is a predictive kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t-1}$,
and $\pi_t$ is a filtering kernel for $X_t$ given $Y_{1:t}$. For each fixed
history $h$, the observation marginal under the conditional version
determined by $\widehat\pi_t(h,\cdot)$ has density
$z_t(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $\nu_t$ and assigns zero mass to both
$\{y:z_t(h,y)=0\}$ and $\{y:z_t(h,y)=\infty\}$. Thus the formula never
divides by zero or infinity; values on those fibers are conditional-law
fillers. The statement is exact and finite-horizon and gives no numerical
approximation or long-time stability claim.

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the finite-horizon target and proposal setting of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For admissible inputs require $\mu_0\ll\nu_0$ and, for each $k\ge1$, $M_k(x,\cdot)\ll R_k(x,\cdot)$ for almost every $x$ under the last-coordinate marginal of the proposal path law $Q_{k-1}$. Select the joint measurable versions $\rho_0=d\mu_0/d\nu_0$ and $r_k(x,\cdot)=dM_k(x,\cdot)/dR_k(x,\cdot)$ supplied by [[thm-feynman-kac-path-radon-nikodym-weight]]. Fix $N\ge1$ and select either multinomial or residual resampling at each time. The algorithm returns a weighted empirical path measure and a normalizer estimate.

1. Draw $X_0^1,\ldots,X_0^N$ independently from $\nu_0$. Set $a_0^i=G_0(X_0^i)\rho_0(X_0^i)$ and $\widehat Z_0=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_0^i$. If $\sum_i a_0^i>0$, put $\bar w_0^i=a_0^i/\sum_j a_0^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_0^i=1/N$. Each initial path is $X_{0:0}^i=X_0^i$.
2. For $k=1,\ldots,t$, do the following:
   1. Apply [[alg-multinomial-and-residual-offspring-resampling]] to the previous normalized weights $(\bar w_{k-1}^1,\ldots,\bar w_{k-1}^N)$, obtaining ancestor indices $A_k^1,\ldots,A_k^N$.
   2. Given the previous paths and these indices, draw $(X_k^1,\ldots,X_k^N)$ with joint conditional law $\bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},\cdot)$ and set $X_{0:k}^i=(X_{0:k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$.
   3. Set $a_k^i=G_k(X_k^i)r_k(X_{k-1}^{A_k^i},X_k^i)$ and $\widehat Z_k=\widehat Z_{k-1}(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Na_k^i)$. If $\sum_i a_k^i>0$, put $\bar w_k^i=a_k^i/\sum_j a_k^j$; otherwise put $\bar w_k^i=1/N$.
3. Return $\widehat Z_t$ and the weighted empirical path probability measure $\widehat\pi_t^N=\sum_{i=1}^N\bar w_t^i\delta_{X_{0:t}^i}$. Its last-coordinate marginal is the corresponding empirical filtering approximation.

The all-zero fallback only defines a probability measure for reporting and future sampling. Once a zero average weight occurs, $\widehat Z$ remains zero. The procedure makes no finite-particle accuracy, consistency, or long-time stability claim.

Input a particle count $N\ge1$, nonnegative finite weights $a_1,\ldots,a_N$, and a scheme label, either multinomial or residual. Let $A=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j$. If $A>0$, set $p_j=a_j/A$; if $A=0$, set $p_j=1/N$ for every $j$. Thus $p$ is always a probability vector.

- **Multinomial scheme.** Draw an index vector $(J_1,\ldots,J_N)\in\{1,\ldots,N\}^N$ with conditional mass $\mathbb P(J_1=j_1,\ldots,J_N=j_N\mid a)=\prod_{\ell=1}^Np_{j_\ell}$. Put $C_j=\#\{\ell:J_\ell=j\}$.
- **Residual scheme.** Put $q_j=\lfloor Np_j\rfloor$, $r_j=Np_j-q_j$, and $R=\sum_{j=1}^Nr_j=N-\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j$, an integer in $\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. If $R=0$, put $C_j=q_j$. For residual resampling, return the ancestor list containing exactly $C_j$ copies of index $j$, ordered by increasing index, together with its count vector. Each output is a length-$N$ list and a count vector summing to $N$. When all input weights vanish, the uniform fallback defines the procedure; any downstream normalizer already multiplied by this zero average remains zero.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\in\mathbb N_0$. For each $0\le k\le T$, let $(\mathsf X_k,\mathcal X_k)$ be a standard Borel space. Let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X_0$, and for $1\le k\le T$ let $M_k:\mathsf X_{k-1}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf X_k$ be a probability kernel. A **potential** at time $k$ is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable function $G_k:\mathsf X_k\to[0,\infty)$. Write $\mathsf X_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^t\mathsf X_k$ with its finite-product sigma-algebra.

For each $0\le t\le T$, let $P_t^M$ be the finite path law with ordered kernel integral $\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{k=1}^tM_k(x_{k-1},dx_k)$, supplied by Ionescu–Tulcea ([[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]]). The **unnormalized Feynman–Kac path measure** is
$$\gamma_t(A)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:t}}\mathbf 1_A(x_{0:t})\prod_{k=0}^tG_k(x_k)\,P_t^M(dx_{0:t}),\qquad A\in\bigotimes_{k=0}^t\mathcal X_k.$$
Its **normalizer** is $Z_t=\gamma_t(\mathsf X_{0:t})=\gamma_t(1)\in[0,\infty]$. Only when $0<Z_t<\infty$ define the normalized path target $\pi_t^{\mathrm{FK}}=\gamma_t/Z_t$. The sequence $(\gamma_t)$ with its kernels and potentials is the Feynman–Kac flow.

State-space filtering kernels are conditional-law versions as in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. A Feynman–Kac path target is not by itself an assertion that a pointwise conditional version has been selected at observation-null histories.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon setup of [[def-feynman-kac-path-targets-and-normalizers]]. For $1\le k\le T$ and every nonnegative product-measurable $\varphi:\mathsf X_{0:k}\to[0,\infty]$,
$$\gamma_k(\varphi)=\int_{\mathsf X_{0:k-1}}\gamma_{k-1}(dx_{0:k-1})\int_{\mathsf X_k}G_k(x_k)\varphi(x_{0:k})M_k(x_{k-1},dx_k),$$
with equality in $[0,\infty]$.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

At time zero, for any bounded continuous $h$, put $V_i=G_0(X_0^i)h(X_0^i)$. Expanding the squared centered sample average, the cross terms vanish by independence and the diagonal terms give $\mathbb E[(
u_0^N(G_0h)-\mu_0(G_0h))^2]\le C^2\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. The same calculation with $V_i=G_0(X_0^i)$ gives the denominator bound $C^2/N$. Applying [F5] to each squared error shows both averages converge in probability to their $\mu_0$ integrals. The denominator limit is at least $c$, so the ratio $\eta_0^N(h)=
u_0^N(G_0h)/
u_0^N(G_0)$ converges in probability to $\mu_0(G_0h)/\mu_0(G_0)=\eta_0(h)$.

Suppose $\eta_{t-1}^N(g)\to\eta_{t-1}(g)$ in probability for every bounded continuous $g$. Conditional on the previous particles, [F1]–[F2] make $X_t^1,\ldots,X_t^N$ IID with common law $\eta_{t-1}^N M_t$. For bounded continuous $h$, the squared error of their empirical average under this product law is the sum of $N$ diagonal centered terms divided by $N^2$; the cross terms vanish by independence, and each diagonal term is at most $\|h\|_\infty^2$. Thus its integral is at most $\|h\|_\infty^2/N$. Applying [F5] under the conditional product law and then integrating over the previous particles gives $\nu_t^N(h)-\eta_{t-1}^N(M_th)\to0$ in probability. The Feller hypothesis makes $M_th$ bounded continuous, so the induction hypothesis gives $\eta_{t-1}^N(M_th)\to\eta_{t-1}(M_th)$.

Apply step 1.2 to $h$ and $G_th$, both bounded continuous. Then $\eta_t^N(h)=\nu_t^N(G_th)/\nu_t^N(G_t)$; the denominator converges to $\eta_{t-1}(M_tG_t)\ge c$. The ratio therefore converges in probability to $\eta_{t-1}(M_t(G_th))/\eta_{t-1}(M_tG_t)=\eta_t(h)$ by [F3]. Induction from step 1.1 proves the assertion for each fixed $t\le T$. The lower bound $c$ rules out zero normalizers, while the upper bound $C$ gives the finite variance bounds used above.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a finite horizon $T\ge0$, fix an integer lag $L\ge0$, a path count
$S\ge1$, and the normalized
filtering particle clouds and transition inputs required by
[[alg-particle-backward-simulator]]. For each time $t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$,
put $s_t=\min(t+L,T)$. Independently for each $t$, run the particle backward
simulator using only the filtering clouds at times $0,\ldots,s_t$ and request
$S$ paths. Retain their time-$t$ coordinates $\widetilde X_t^{t,1},\ldots,
\widetilde X_t^{t,S}$ and return the empirical measure
$$\widehat\eta_{t|s_t}^{S}=\frac1S\sum_{r=1}^S\delta_{\widetilde X_t^{t,r}}.$$
In particle mode this empirical law approximates
$$\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:s_t}),$$
not the full smoothing law $\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:T})$ unless $s_t=T$ or
the two conditional laws happen to agree. The same procedure can use supplied
exact backward kernels when the model has no transition density; for each
$s_t$ it uses the supplied filtering kernel at $y_{1:s_t}$ and the backward
kernels for the corresponding prefix histories. On histories where these
kernels factor the truncated smoother, it samples that exact conditional law.

The procedure returns one truncated smoothing marginal per $t$. It does not
assert a bound on the lag bias, a forgetting rate, or convergence to the
full-data smoother for fixed $L$. Those conclusions require separate
conditions on the model.

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.

$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$

$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$

$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$

successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density

Since $\lambda_{t+1}$ is a probability measure, $|M_{t+1}h(x_n)-M_{t+1}h(x)|\le\|h\|_\infty\sup_{x'}|f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_n)-f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)|\to0.$ Thus each transition is Feller.

For each $0\le t<T$, put $q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\eta_t(dx)$ and $q_{t+1}^N(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\eta_t^N(dx)$. The density bounds imply $a\le q_{t+1}(x'),q_{t+1}^N(x')\le b$ for every $x'$, so every backward denominator used by the algorithm is finite positive.

Fix $0\le t<T$ and a continuous $h$ on $E_t$. The families $x\mapsto f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ and $x\mapsto h(x)f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ indexed by $x'\in E_{t+1}$ are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous: joint continuity on the compact product is uniformly continuous. For any $\epsilon>0$, a finite $\epsilon$-net of the compact parameter space gives a finite sup-norm net for each family. Weak convergence in probability from step 2.1 gives convergence of the integrals for every function in each finite net; since all measures have mass one, replacing a family member by a net function changes either integral by at most $\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves uniform-in-$x'$ convergence of both numerators and denominators. Division is stable because all denominators are at least $a$, so $\sup_{x'}|B_t^N h(x')-B_th(x')|\to0$ in probability for the empirical and exact backward kernels. The exact function $B_th$ is continuous by dominated convergence.

For each $0\le t<T$, set $\omega_f(\delta)=\sup_{x,x',x'' : d(x',x'')\le\delta}|f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)-f_{t+1}(x''\mid x)|$, which tends to zero by uniform continuity. The exact and empirical backward kernels have densities $f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)/q_{t+1}(x')$ relative to $\eta_t$ and $f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)/q_{t+1}^N(x')$ relative to $\eta_t^N$, respectively. Using [F2]–[F3], $q,q^N\in[a,b]$ from step 2.1, and that both filtering measures have mass one, their total-variation distance at $x',x''$ is at most $\omega_f(\delta)(a^{-1}+ba^{-2})$. Since $T$ is finite, iterating this estimate yields one such class for every section in the finite telescoping sum.

Telescope the finite backward product by replacing one empirical kernel at a time with its exact counterpart. The uniform moduli from step 3.2 put every possible section, over all clouds and remaining coordinates, in a uniformly bounded equicontinuous class on a compact metric space. The same finite-net argument and [F1] give convergence of the terminal empirical integrals uniformly over the resulting class. Thus every term in the finite telescoping sum tends to zero in probability, and the conditional path law $\widehat\psi_T^N$ converges weakly in the sense of [F4] to the exact product law $\psi_T$ in [F2].

[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and

the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that

composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular

random element is its data-indexed kernel form in

successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density

$$q_{t+1}^N(x')=\sum_{i:w_t^i>0}w_t^i f_{t+1}(x'\mid x_t^i).$$

$S$ paths. Retain their time-$t$ coordinates $\widetilde X_t^{t,1},\ldots,

$$\widehat\eta_{t|s_t}^{S}=\frac1S\sum_{r=1}^S\delta_{\widetilde X_t^{t,r}}.$$
In particle mode this empirical law approximates
$$\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:s_t}),$$
not the full smoothing law $\mathcal L(X_t\mid Y_{1:T})$ unless $s_t=T$ or

The procedure returns one truncated smoothing marginal per $t$. It does not

Assume AC, a finite-horizon Markov state-space model with standard-Borel
states, dominated observation kernels, and data-indexed filtering and
smoothing kernels as in
[[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. Fix an observation history
$y_{1:T}$ in the full-measure set where the dominated filtering recursion
[[thm-dominated-state-space-filtering-recursion]] applies. Write $\eta_t$
for the filtering law of $X_t$ given $y_{1:t}$. Suppose the transition kernel
$M_{t+1}$ from time $t$ to $t+1$ has a product-measurable density
$f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)$ with respect to a sigma-finite measure $\lambda_{t+1}$,
meaning
$$M_{t+1}(x,A)=\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\lambda_{t+1}(dx')$$
for every state $x$ and measurable set $A$.
Put
$$q_{t+1}(x')=\int f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx),\qquad D_{t+1}=\{x':0<q_{t+1}(x')<\infty\}.$$
The backward conditional kernel is
$$B_t(x',A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A f_{t+1}(x'\mid x)\,\eta_t(dx)}{q_{t+1}(x')},&x'\in D_{t+1},\\\eta_t(A),&x'\notin D_{t+1}.\end{cases}$$
It is a probability-kernel version of the conditional law of $X_t$ given
$X_{t+1}=x'$ and $y_{1:t}$. The finite-horizon smoothing kernel factors as
$$\psi_T(dx_{0:T})=\eta_T(dx_T)\prod_{t=T-1}^{0}B_t(x_{t+1},dx_t)$$
for observation-almost every full history, with the product interpreted as
successive backwards kernel integration. If the transition is supplied only
as a probability kernel, the same factorization uses a supplied regular
conditional kernel of $X_t$ given $(X_{t+1},Y_{1:t})$; no transition density
is asserted in that case. Null-history values remain version-dependent.
